data.title: Aristote à Bagdad: Catégories et Métaphysique
data.abstractNote: Cet article revient sur les rapports entre catégories et métaphysique chez les aristotéliciens de Bagdad. Contre les grammairiens contemporains, l'école de Bagdad a développé une interprétation métaphysique des catégories. Dans ses traités théologiques, Yaḥyâ ibn 'Adî exhibe une multiplicité de «choses» (ashyâ') et d'«intentions» (ma'ânî) dans une même «substance» (jawhar). Ces deux concepts se retrouvent chez al-Fârâbî convoquant dans son Kitâb al-ḥurûf les catégories pour mettre en place une métaphysique. La «chose» que considère la métaphysique se laisse alors appréhender à partir de ce qui se donne à penser. This paper provides a presentation of the relations between categories and metaphysics according to the Baghdadian aristotelians. Against the contemporary grammarians, the school of Baghdad have proposed a metaphysical interpretation of the categories. In his theological tractates, Yaḥyâ ibn 'Adî discovers a multiplicity of "things" (ashyâ) and of "intentions" (ma'ânî) in a single "substance" (jawhar). Al-Fârâbî uses too these two concepts when he establishes, in his Kitâb al-hurûfi a metaphysics based on the categories. In this way, metaphysics deals not only with beings, but also with "things", which are things thought.

data.title: The Long Genocide in Upper Mesopotamia: Minority Population Destruction amidst Nation-Building and ‘International Security’
data.abstractNote: “Genocide in Kurdistan” most often refers to events that are recognized as having occurred in Iraq during the late 1980s and early 1990s. Scholars also connect it with events in Turkey’s early years as a republic. This article describes how some scholars’ expansive conception of Kurdistan encompasses regions that also witnessed genocides as large as or larger (in quantitative terms) than these two cases. Armenians, Assyrians, Yezidis, Mandaeans, Shi’i Arabs, and Greek Orthodox Christians witnessed extermination campaigns at various points in Ottoman, Persian, Iraqi, and Turkish history. What is remarkable about Upper Mesopotamia is that these genocides may have reduced native populations in absolute numbers, as compared with ancient or early medieval figures, and to a greater extent than after the genocides of the Kurds or other groups. Like the work of Raphael Lemkin, this article’s analysis will not be limited to the period since the Genocide Convention entered into force. Instead, it presents evidence of continuities between the denationalization strategies, official pretexts, and regions mentioned in histories of the various genocides in Upper Mesopotamia.

data.title: A Critical Evaluation of the Syriac Version of the Psalms of Solomon
data.abstractNote: This study attempts to determine the place of the Syriac version of the Psalms of Solomon within the textual tradition of this 1st c. B.C.E. Jewish pseudepigraphon and, thus, to assess the relative value of the Syriac version over against the Greek version as a textual witness for the Psalms of Solomon. In Chapter I, the need for this study is established. Although scholars have long recognized the importance of the Psalms of Solomon and have agreed that the Psalms of Solomon are extant only in translation of what was probably a Hebrew original, the Syriac version, one of only two versions of the Psalms of Solomon known to exist, has been largely denigrated as a textual witness and often ignored completely. Indeed, no one has made a comprehensive investigation into the textual value of the Syriac version. In Chapter II, the five extant Syriac and eleven extant Greek manuscripts of the Psalms of Solomon are identified. In Chapter III, the Syriac and the Greek versions are compared. For each of the eighteen psalms, the Syriac and the Greek texts are set forth in parallel columns on facing pages, followed by a translation of the Syriac, notes dealing with the character of the Syriac and with differences between the Syriac and the Greek, and a summary. In Chapter IV, an attempt to ascertain the Vorlage of the Syr is made. First, the evidence which might imply a Greek Vorlage for the Syriac is collected and then evaluated critically. Next, the evidence which might imply a Heb Vorlage is collected and then evaluated critically. Finally, it is concluded that the evidence for a Hebrew Vorlage is stronger than that for a Greek. In Chapter V, the relative value of the Syriac version as a textual witness to the Psalms of Solomon is discussed. A tabulation of passages where the Syriac seems to preserve the original reading of the text over against the Greek, and vice-versa, suggests two conclusions: first, that the extant Syriac tradition is an important witness to the text and cannot be ignored; and, second, that the extant Greek tradition is, overall, a better textual witness than the Syriac with respect to the meaning of the text. In Chapter VI, the results of this study are summarized and the importance of both the Syriac and the Greek versions as textual witnesses to the Psalms of Solomon is reaffirmed.
